proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.rationale: Clicking helps resolve an information gap while preserving enough context to make the gap intelligible.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline makes the reader want a missing outcome or explanation while remaining understandable. Scores low when it states the complete takeaway or is merely opaque; does not apply without an implied information gap.

proposals.name: Plain-language clarity
proposals.rationale: Readership favors headlines that reduce processing effort and make the story immediately legible.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the subject, action, and meaning are immediately clear in ordinary language. Scores low when wording is ambiguous, compressed, or jargon-heavy; does not apply when the headline makes no substantive proposition.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.rationale: Strong emotions increase attention and sharing even when traditional news-value signals are weak.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline conveys strong fear, anger, joy, tenderness, or disgust. Scores low when it is emotionally neutral; does not apply without a discernible emotional cue.

proposals.name: Personal consequence
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize stories affecting their lives, beyond aggregate economic or domestic significance.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the subject plausibly affects an ordinary reader’s own health, safety, money, rights, or family. Scores low when consequences are remote or abstract; does not apply without a personal implication.

proposals.name: Moral transgression
proposals.rationale: Moral transgression invites judgment and discussion, generating interest beyond the presence of legal proceedings.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline presents taboo, betrayal, injustice, exploitation, or scandal. Scores low when it describes routine or norm-consistent behavior; does not apply without a clear conduct or norm signal.

proposals.name: Interpersonal conflict
proposals.rationale: Social contests attract follow-up attention even without crisis, violence, or institutional action.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when identifiable people or groups oppose, accuse, reject, or challenge one another. Scores low when relationships are cooperative or non-adversarial; does not apply without explicit antagonism.

proposals.name: Unresolved trajectory
proposals.rationale: Pending outcomes create a reason to click now and return for resolution.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a decision, result, threat, or consequence remains pending and invites monitoring. Scores low when the event and outcome are settled; does not apply without temporal progression.

proposals.name: Cultural touchstone
proposals.rationale: Shared references lower recognition costs and broaden the potential audience.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline invokes a widely recognizable cultural object, phrase, franchise, or shared reference. Scores low when the reference is obscure; does not apply without a cultural referent.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.rationale: Explanatory framing motivates information-seeking beyond simple event awareness.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the wording promises to explain why, how, or what happened. Scores low when it merely announces an event; does not apply without an implied explanatory question.

proposals.name: Direct personal voice
proposals.rationale: Direct voice supplies authenticity and emotional immediacy, strengthening reader engagement.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a first-person admission, plea, testimony, or strongly voiced quotation is central. Scores low when the headline is impersonal summary; does not apply without a human speaker.

proposals.name: Humorous framing
proposals.rationale: Playful framing can attract clicks despite low conventional news value.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline uses wit, wordplay, comic contrast, or playful absurdity. Scores low when its tone is strictly literal or formal; does not apply without a playful cue.

proposals.name: Visual imaginability
proposals.rationale: Concrete imagery improves memorability and mental simulation, supporting spontaneous readership.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline evokes a concrete scene, object, or action that is easy to picture. Scores low when it is abstract or bureaucratic; does not apply when it lacks concrete content.

proposals.name: Actionable utility
proposals.rationale: Practical guidance gives readers immediate instrumental value, distinct from general interest.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the story appears to offer advice, protection, instructions, or decision-relevant information. Scores low when it offers no practical takeaway; does not apply without an implied action or choice.

proposals.name: Identity resonance
proposals.rationale: Identity-relevant stories invite self-placement and group discussion beyond event magnitude.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline invites identification with or judgment of a religious, ethnic, national, sexual, or political group. Scores low when it is socially impersonal; does not apply without an identity-bearing group.

proposals.name: Narrative coherence
proposals.rationale: Coherent mini-narratives are easier to process and mentally complete, encouraging readers to enter the story.
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline forms a compact story with an agent, action, and consequence or tension. Scores low when it is fragmentary, list-like, or overloaded; does not apply when too little content supports a narrative.

proposals.name: Headline length band
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count the words; mark yes for a headline of six words or fewer.

proposals.name: Colon-led topic label
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Begins with a short label followed by a colon and a proposition.

proposals.name: Interrogative packaging
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Begins with “how,” “why,” “what,” “will,” or “can” and poses a question.

proposals.name: Promotion or media tag
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Contains a label such as “live,” “watch,” “video,” “explained,” or “in pictures.”

proposals.name: Continuation or sequence cue
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Explicitly signals sequence or continuation, such as “day 18,” “still,” “again,” or “what now.”

proposals.name: Calendar or daypart wording
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Names a weekday, holiday, season, date, or time of day.

proposals.name: Wire-style attribution syntax
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Uses source-first wording such as “police say,” “X says,” or “boss warns.”

proposals.name: Acronym-heavy casing
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Contains at least two all-uppercase abbreviations, such as “US,” “UN,” or “DR.”

proposals.name: Scare-quote packaging
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Places a single evaluative word or short phrase in quotation marks without presenting a full quotation.

proposals.name: First-person or plea framing
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Uses “I,” “we,” “me,” or “my,” or directly frames a personal plea.

proposals.name: Immediate Clarity
proposals.rationale: Clear headlines reduce comprehension costs and make clicking more likely.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline clearly identifies who did what and why; low when elliptical, vague, or metaphorical. Does not apply when the wording provides no recoverable event structure.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.rationale: Unresolved information can motivate readers to click for completion.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline withholds a salient answer while implying one exists; low when it fully resolves the story or supplies no hook. Does not apply without an implied unanswered question.

proposals.name: Emotional Language
proposals.rationale: Explicit emotion can attract attention beyond institutional or event severity.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording explicitly conveys fear, outrage, wonder, shame, grief, or delight; low when emotionally neutral. Does not apply when affect is supplied only by the underlying event category.

proposals.name: Personal Actionability
proposals.rationale: Practical utility can drive readership independently of domestic relevance.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline suggests information useful for an individual decision or behavior; low when no personal response is imaginable. Does not apply without a plausible reader-facing action or implication.

proposals.name: Moral Identity Contest
proposals.rationale: Identity-relevant disagreement can generate strong reader motivation and discussion.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline challenges a group identity, taboo, or moral norm; low when it merely describes facts. Does not apply when no value-laden identity or norm is invoked.

proposals.name: First-Person Disclosure
proposals.rationale: Personal disclosure creates immediacy distinct from generic human-interest content.
proposals.description: Scores high when a quoted speaker reveals personal experience, feeling, motive, or confession; low when no intimate voice appears. Does not apply when quotation is only an official factual statement.

proposals.name: Visual Vividness
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental imagery can increase attention and memorability.
proposals.description: Scores high when the words evoke a concrete, easily pictured scene, object, or action; low when abstract or bureaucratic. Does not apply when the headline contains no imageable content.

proposals.name: Goal Conflict
proposals.rationale: Interpersonal or ideological contest can attract clicks without requiring crisis or violence.
proposals.description: Scores high when opposing parties, positions, or objectives are explicitly juxtaposed; low when the headline presents one-sided activity. Does not apply when no competing aims or claims are stated.

proposals.name: Expectation Reversal
proposals.rationale: Structural surprise may engage readers beyond ordinary novelty.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline signals an outcome contrary to an apparent expectation, especially through reversal or contradiction. Does not apply when no expectation can be inferred from the wording.

proposals.name: Future Uncertainty
proposals.rationale: Uncertain consequences can sustain reader interest independently of current crisis.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline foregrounds an unresolved consequence, conditional future, or “what happens next” problem; low when the outcome is settled. Does not apply when no future state is implicated.

proposals.name: Verification Cue
proposals.rationale: Credibility signals can make a claim worth investigating.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline references footage, records, data, fact-checking, testimony, or another evidentiary basis; low when it presents an unsupported assertion. Does not apply when no evidence or sourcing cue appears.

proposals.name: Semantic Accessibility
proposals.rationale: Accessible wording broadens the potential readership beyond topic specialists.
proposals.description: Scores high when ordinary vocabulary and familiar references permit understanding without specialist knowledge; low when jargon or obscure terminology dominates. Does not apply when accessibility cannot be judged from the headline alone.

proposals.name: Cultural Resonance
proposals.rationale: Shared references can create recognition and personal relevance without relying on celebrity.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline invokes a widely shared cultural text, ritual, symbol, or historical reference; low when culturally unanchored. Does not apply when no shared cultural cue is present.

proposals.name: Consequence Specificity
proposals.rationale: Specific consequences help readers judge why the story matters.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline states a concrete result, change, or implication; low when it uses generic verbs such as “warns” or “faces pressure.” Does not apply when no consequence is asserted or implied.

proposals.name: Conversation Potential
proposals.rationale: Anticipated discussion can increase readership independently of listed news values.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline presents a compact, quotable claim likely to invite agreement, disagreement, or sharing; low when it is routine and non-evaluative. Does not apply without a proposition or viewpoint to react to.

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count words and clauses; unusually compressed or expansive headlines may reflect slot space, not reader appeal.

proposals.name: Interrogative framing
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag headlines framed as a question or beginning with “How,” “Why,” or “What.” This may reflect explainer packaging rather than underlying readership merit.

proposals.name: Quoted first-person voice
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag a first-person statement or direct personal quotation, especially with an “I” construction. This can identify interview or feature packaging independent of article appeal.

proposals.name: Teaser punctuation
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag quotation marks around vague or evaluative words, ellipses, dashes, or other teaser-like punctuation. Such formatting may be a house-style or curiosity device.

proposals.name: Place-name density
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count explicit countries, cities, regions, or demonyms in the headline. Geographic density may reveal assignment desk or bureau origin rather than readership merit.

proposals.name: Legal-procedural diction
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag terms such as “court,” “arrest,” “ruling,” “trial,” “accused,” or “guilty.” These may proxy the legal or crime beat.

proposals.name: Political office titles
proposals.parent: politics desk and political news cycle
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count formal political or institutional titles such as president, PM, senator, or congressman. This may reflect politics-desk production and packaging.

proposals.name: Human-interest vocabulary
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag family, child, grandmother, plea, personal revelation, or similarly intimate wording. Such wording may identify feature-desk staffing or a soft-news template.

proposals.name: Running-story continuity cues
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag “still,” “again,” “day N,” “what now,” or other wording that presupposes an earlier story. These cues may encode persistence in a multi-day news run.

proposals.name: Wire-copy boilerplate
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Flag formulaic constructions such as “X says,” “X denies,” “X to visit,” or “X found at Y,” with minimal descriptive variation. This may identify syndicated or routine desk copy.

proposals.name: IMMEDIATE COMPREHENSIBILITY
proposals.rationale: Lower processing effort makes a headline more likely to convert homepage exposure into a click.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording is instantly understandable on first reading, and low when syntax or vocabulary requires rereading. Does not apply when the headline is too fragmentary to judge.

proposals.name: CONCRETE SPECIFICITY
proposals.rationale: Specific details help readers assess relevance and distinguish compelling stories from generic news.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline names specific actors, actions, objects, places, or numbers, and low when it relies on generic abstractions. Does not apply when semantic content is insufficient.

proposals.name: CURIOSITY GAP
proposals.rationale: A bounded information gap creates a reason to open the article.
proposals.description: Scores high when a concrete question or outcome is deliberately left unresolved, and low when the headline fully resolves the central question or is merely vague. Does not apply without an implied information gap.

proposals.name: EXPLANATORY PAYOFF
proposals.rationale: Readers click when the headline promises understanding, not merely another event notice.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline promises causes, meaning, or implications, and low when it merely announces an event. Does not apply when no apparent explanatory question exists.

proposals.name: PERSONAL SELF-RELEVANCE
proposals.rationale: Perceived personal relevance is a direct motivation for readership.
proposals.description: Scores high when ordinary readers can readily connect the topic to their own lives, and low when relevance is remote or specialized. Does not apply when the headline gives no basis for judging audience relevance.

proposals.name: EMOTIONAL VIVIDNESS
proposals.rationale: Affective activation can attract attention beyond formal news-value signals.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording or circumstances evoke a strong feeling beyond formal crisis or violence, and low when affect is flat or purely administrative. Does not apply to emotionally neutral wording.

proposals.name: IDENTITY RESONANCE
proposals.rationale: Group-linked stakes can mobilize readership without elite actors or domestic relevance.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline invokes a recognizable social, national, political, religious, or generational identity with value stakes, and low when no identity is salient. Does not apply when relevant identities are unstated.

proposals.name: MORAL EVALUATION
proposals.rationale: Clear moral meaning can trigger interest, judgment, and sharing.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline clearly signals wrongdoing, injustice, betrayal, vindication, compassion, or admiration, and low when it is morally neutral. Does not apply when judgment derives only from legal status or violence.

proposals.name: NARRATIVE TENSION
proposals.rationale: Unresolved goals and obstacles invite readers to learn what happens next.
proposals.description: Scores high when identifiable goals, obstacles, or opposing forces remain unresolved, and low when the headline describes a static or completed state. Does not apply without discernible actors or objectives.

proposals.name: PRACTICAL UTILITY
proposals.rationale: Actionable implications give readers a concrete reason to seek more information.
proposals.description: Scores high when the article appears likely to inform a decision, action, precaution, or behavior, and low when it offers no usable implication. Does not apply when no decision-relevant consequence is suggested.

proposals.name: EVIDENCE CUES
proposals.rationale: Verification cues increase trust and interest in checking the underlying story.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline signals footage, records, fact-checking, data, or credible attribution, and low when it presents an unsupported assertion. Does not apply when evidence is irrelevant to the claim.

proposals.name: ACCOUNTABILITY CLARITY
proposals.rationale: Clear responsibility makes consequences easier to understand and follow.
proposals.description: Scores high when a specific actor is clearly linked to an action and consequence, and low when responsibility is passive, anonymous, or diffuse. Does not apply when the story involves no assignable responsibility.

proposals.name: VISUAL SCENEABILITY
proposals.rationale: Easy-to-imagine scenes improve salience and memorability on a crowded homepage.
proposals.description: Scores high when the wording readily evokes a concrete, imaginable scene, and low when it remains abstract or conceptual. Does not apply when the subject cannot plausibly be visualized from the headline.

proposals.name: CONTEXT INDEPENDENCE
proposals.rationale: Standalone intelligibility prevents prior-story knowledge from becoming a click prerequisite.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline is intelligible without prior knowledge, and low when it depends on unexplained references or earlier coverage. Does not apply when necessary context is explicitly supplied.

proposals.name: PERSONAL AGENCY
proposals.rationale: Individual choice and consequence create a compact, legible narrative hook.
proposals.description: Scores high when an identifiable individual makes an unusual choice, refusal, admission, or appeal with consequences, and low when individuals are merely mentioned. Does not apply when no individual agency is expressed.

proposals.name: Headline brevity
proposals.description: Count whether the headline is unusually short or compressed, excluding spaces and punctuation.

proposals.name: Template punctuation
proposals.description: Mark headlines using a colon, dash, question mark, or quoted phrase in a recognizable house-style template.

proposals.name: Explainer framing
proposals.description: Mark “why,” “how,” “what now,” or similarly explicit explanatory framing.

proposals.name: Celebrity-name anchor
proposals.description: Mark a headline centered on a named entertainer, athlete, or other celebrity.

proposals.name: Domestic shorthand
proposals.description: Mark UK-audience shorthand such as “PM,” “UK,” or locally familiar institutional references.

proposals.name: International-place density
proposals.parent: International desk, time zone, or correspondent availability
proposals.description: Count prominent foreign countries, cities, or regions named in the headline.

proposals.name: Running-story marker
proposals.description: Mark explicit continuation cues such as “still,” “again,” “day 18,” “after,” or “what now.”

proposals.name: Calendar-era vocabulary
proposals.description: Mark references to Covid, Christmas, elections, or other calendar-specific events that date the headline.

proposals.name: Interview-voice quotation
proposals.description: Mark a headline built around a first-person statement or a distinctive person’s quoted words.

proposals.name: Colloquial sensational wording
proposals.description: Mark conspicuously vivid, playful, emotional, or conversational wording rather than neutral description.

proposals.name: Concrete information gap
proposals.rationale: Unresolved questions create a direct click motive without depending on editorial prominence.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline poses or implies a specific unanswered question a click could resolve; score low when it gives a complete, settled account. Do not apply when no meaningful question is inferable.

proposals.name: Outcome or resolution payoff
proposals.rationale: Readers may click to obtain closure, even when the topic lacks classic news value.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline states a discovery, verdict, rescue, cancellation, or other consequential outcome; score low when no result is provided. Do not apply when no event outcome is described.

proposals.name: Evidence or reveal cue
proposals.rationale: Reveals and verification offer informational value beyond ordinary event reporting.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline promises hidden evidence, verification, admission, or a newly uncovered record; score low when it merely asserts a position. Do not apply when no disclosure or evidence cue appears.

proposals.name: Explicit causal linkage
proposals.rationale: Causal coherence helps readers understand why an event matters and motivates explanatory clicks.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline clearly states why one event produces another; score low when it merely juxtaposes facts. Do not apply when causation is not central to the story.

proposals.name: Concrete scene imagery
proposals.rationale: Vivid imagery makes unfamiliar stories mentally accessible and memorable.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline depicts a specific action, place, object, or observable scene; score low when it uses only abstract concepts. Do not apply when no scene detail is present.

proposals.name: Self-contained context
proposals.rationale: Self-contained headlines reduce comprehension costs for broad same-site readership.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline identifies enough actors, events, and circumstances to understand its premise; score low when it depends on unexplained references or prior coverage. Do not apply when contextual sufficiency cannot be judged.

proposals.name: Plain-language accessibility
proposals.rationale: Accessibility increases the number of readers who can immediately understand the click proposition.
proposals.description: Score high when wording is familiar, direct, and syntactically simple; score low when it relies on jargon, convoluted syntax, or obscure references. Do not apply when specialized terminology is unavoidable and clearly explained.

proposals.name: Practical personal utility
proposals.rationale: Direct usefulness can drive readership independently of economic impact or domestic relevance.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline implies usable consequences for personal safety, rights, health, travel, or finances; score low when no personal decision is suggested. Do not apply when reader action is not inferable.

proposals.name: First-hand testimony
proposals.rationale: First-hand voice can create identification and trust beyond generic human-interest framing.
proposals.description: Score high when an affected person gives a first-person account, plea, or disclosure; score low when the headline offers only an impersonal summary. Do not apply when the quotation is merely an official position.

proposals.name: Explicit interpersonal clash
proposals.rationale: Legible conflict supplies narrative tension without requiring violence, crisis, or legal proceedings.
proposals.description: Score high when named people or groups directly disagree, accuse, reject, or challenge one another; score low when only one position appears. Do not apply when disagreement is merely inferred.

proposals.name: Expectation reversal
proposals.rationale: Reversals create cognitive tension that can attract clicks independently of general novelty.
proposals.description: Score high when wording signals a contradiction or reversal against an implied expectation, such as “despite,” “still,” or “but”; score low for straightforward developments. Do not apply when no baseline expectation is visible.

proposals.name: Consequential uncertainty
proposals.rationale: Uncertainty with stakes encourages monitoring behavior beyond generic recency.
proposals.description: Score high when future or conditional wording is paired with a specified possible consequence; score low for forecasts without meaningful stakes. Do not apply when no future contingency is present.

proposals.name: Emotional immediacy
proposals.rationale: Immediate affect can trigger attention without requiring celebrity, violence, or human-interest framing.
proposals.description: Score high when the headline contains an explicit plea, fear, grief, anger, shame, or other strong affect; score low when emotionally neutral. Do not apply when emotional wording is incidental.

proposals.name: Memorable verbal packaging
proposals.rationale: Memorable language helps a headline stand out among competing stories.
proposals.description: Score high when an understandable idiom, metaphor, pun, or striking phrase makes the headline distinctive; score low for boilerplate wording. Do not apply when no salient phrasing appears.

proposals.name: Local specificity plus universal stakes
proposals.rationale: Concrete entry points combined with broad relevance can expand readership beyond directly affected audiences.
proposals.description: Score high when a concrete person or place is paired with a clearly general human consequence; score low when either element is absent. Do not apply when neither level is visible.

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count the headline’s words; unusually short or long headlines form a measurable format proxy.

proposals.name: Quotation-mark framing
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark whether the headline contains quoted speech or scare quotes.

proposals.name: Question or explainer form
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines phrased as questions or explicit “what/why/how” explainers.

proposals.name: Curiosity-gap wording
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines that withhold the central referent or outcome, using vague hooks such as “what now,” “episode,” or “two parts.”

proposals.name: Named-person lead
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines beginning with a specific person’s name, title, or celebrity identity.

proposals.name: Institutional-action boilerplate
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark formulaic constructions such as “court blocks,” “president says,” “UN urges,” or “police find.”

proposals.name: International place-name density
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Count countries, cities, regions, or demonyms appearing in the headline, especially multiple such references.

proposals.name: Numerals and scale quantifiers
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark digits, ordinals, and terms such as “hundreds,” “thousands,” “largest,” or “top.”

proposals.name: Personal and emotional framing
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark kinship terms, pleas, first-person testimony, vulnerability, or strongly affective adjectives.

proposals.name: Running-story installment markers
proposals.parent: story age and position in a multi-day news run
proposals.description: DESCRIPTION: Mark explicit continuation cues such as “day 18,” “still,” “after,” “remains,” or “what now.”

proposals.name: Direct Audience Addressing
proposals.rationale: Personal pronouns forge an immediate psychological connection, strongly driving reader click-through rates.
proposals.description: Headlines using first or second person pronouns (I, we, you) score high; third-person or objective headlines score low.

proposals.name: Clickbait Information Gap
proposals.rationale: Exploiting the curiosity gap heavily incentivizes readers to click to resolve uncertainty.
proposals.description: Headlines framing a mystery or withheld revelation (e.g., "What happened", "Why") score high; explicit factual statements score low.

proposals.name: Narrative Suspense Phrasing
proposals.rationale: Emotional suspense creates a powerful urge to click and uncover the missing context.
proposals.description: Headlines using delayed reveals or cliffhanger syntax (e.g., "felt like an earthquake") score high; fully resolved statements score low.

proposals.name: Subjectively Vague Subject
proposals.rationale: Vague but alarming nouns entice users to click for clarifying specifics not provided upfront.
proposals.description: Headlines lacking a specific named entity but using emotive nouns (e.g., "Collapse") score high; precise, comprehensive subjects score low.

proposals.name: Identity Politics Conflict
proposals.rationale: Readers frequently click on polarizing cultural issues that resonate with their personal identity.
proposals.description: Headlines highlighting progressive versus conservative cultural disputes (e.g., abortion, gays, guns) score high; neutral policy headlines score low.

proposals.name: Viral Digital Scams
proposals.rationale: Readers engage heavily with personal digital security threats and viral internet phenomena.
proposals.description: Headlines mentioning hacking, online scams, or internet security flaws score high; physical infrastructure failures score low.

proposals.name: Bizarre Juxtaposition
proposals.rationale: Absurd or highly unusual combinations trigger intense curiosity, boosting user clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines combining unlikely concepts (e.g., "Congressman" and "comic") score high; traditional institutional pairings score low.

proposals.name: Child Vulnerability Hook
proposals.rationale: Evolutionary psychology makes threats to children highly salient, driving immediate reader engagement.
proposals.description: Headlines centering on the peril, exploitation, or targeting of a child score high; adult-focused vulnerability headlines score low.

proposals.name: Hard News Geography Overload
proposals.rationale: Cognitive load from multiple foreign names reduces casual reader interest and click-through rates.
proposals.description: Headlines naming multiple non-Western regions or complex foreign conflicts score low; domestic or single-named regions score high.

proposals.name: Localized Impact Framing
proposals.rationale: Readers click more often when an issue is framed as affecting their daily life directly.
proposals.description: Headlines framing foreign or political issues through a direct, everyday lens (e.g., "your security") score high; abstract political analysis scores low.

proposals.name: Visual Secret Evidence
proposals.rationale: The promise of viewing exclusive, illicit, or visual proof is a powerful click driver.
proposals.description: Headlines explicitly mentioning hidden or leaked footage score high; standard investigative reports or summaries score low.

proposals.name: Technological Disruption
proposals.rationale: Tech and crypto stories draw high engagement from young, digitally native news consumers.
proposals.description: Headlines focusing on cryptocurrency, app-based services, or digital disruption score high; traditional corporate earnings score low.

proposals.name: Direct Impact Warning
proposals.rationale: Future threats create urgency, compelling users to click to ensure their own awareness.
proposals.description: Headlines predicting imminent disaster or mass societal disruption (e.g., "new threat") score high; past-tense analytical stories score low.

proposals.name: Outgroup Antagonism
proposals.rationale: Readers engage strongly with conflict and stories validating their grievances against political opponents.
proposals.description: Headlines highlighting ideological resistance or mocking of elites (e.g., "takes swipe") score high; polite institutional discourse scores low.

proposals.name: Medical Maltreatment
proposals.rationale: Institutional medical failures trigger deep personal anxieties, prompting immediate reader investigation.
proposals.description: Headlines emphasizing botched healthcare, wrong results, or medical testing failures score high; standard policy health news scores low.

proposals.name: Story sequence marker
proposals.description: Headline starts with a temporal day-count (e.g., "day 18") or references ongoing continuity (e.g., "what now for").

proposals.name: Continuing news verb
proposals.description: Uses verbs indicating ongoing evolution rather than a discrete event (e.g., "remains," "takes shine off").

proposals.name: Reader-roadmap interrogative
proposals.description: Formatted as a forward-looking question starting with "How," "Why," or "What."

proposals.name: Punchy single quote marker
proposals.description: Headline features a brief, sensational single quote (e.g., 'unacceptable', 'colossal').

proposals.name: Exceptionalism framing device
proposals.description: Uses specific phrasing to highlight stark contrast or irony (e.g., "despite," "but," "still").

proposals.name: Appositive name emphasis
proposals.description: Places a subject's name before a colon to introduce a personal quote or revelation (e.g., "Harry:", "Robinhood boss:").

proposals.name: Regional geopolitics lexicon
proposals.description: Highlights institutional actions in non-Western regions using terms like "court blocks," "urged to," or "backs."

proposals.name: Syndicated feature syntax
proposals.description: Uses colloquial idioms or slang (e.g., "wrong 'un," "takes swipe") indicating a softer human interest feature.

proposals.name: Entanglement booster phrase
proposals.description: Includes text explicitly linking separate major news cycles or topics (e.g., "Coronavirus halts...").

proposals.name: Bureaucratic event marker
proposals.description: References abstract institutional processes without named individuals (e.g., "Georgia voter fraud claims").

proposals.name: High-recognition celebrity or named individual
proposals.rationale: Readers exhibit strong click bias toward highly recognizable, famous personalities over institutional actors.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline names a globally recognizable celebrity, royal, or prominent individual. Scores low if the subjects are only foreign officials or unknown civilians.

proposals.name: Direct quotation or sensational first-person claim
proposals.rationale: Direct quotes create intimate curiosity and promise exclusive personal details, driving higher reader clicks.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline features a direct quote or first-person confession. Scores low if it is a standard third-person report.

proposals.name: UK-centric novelty or quirky local event
proposals.rationale: The BBC's domestic audience heavily clicks on relatable, idiosyncratic local news over serious foreign politics.
proposals.description: Scores high for distinctly British cultural events, local quirks, or unusual domestic community stories. Scores low for foreign affairs or broad global trends.

proposals.name: Recreational internet or tech controversy
proposals.rationale: Digital native readers disproportionately click on stories about the platforms and cultural debates they use daily.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text references social media, viral memes, streaming platforms, or internet culture. Scores low for traditional politics or hardware.

proposals.name: Bizarre visual premise or absurd literal claim
proposals.rationale: Audiences click absurd or bizarre literal headlines for entertainment and shock value, seeking visual confirmation.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text explicitly describes a visually absurd, comical, or physically unusual situation. Scores low for standard diplomatic or legal actions.

proposals.name: Graphic body violation or visceral violence
proposals.rationale: Visceral violence or bodily violation triggers strong morbid curiosity, sparking more reader clicks than abstract institutional events.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text contains visceral, graphic bodily terms like rape, caning, or trafficking. Scores low for bloodless institutional violence like 'sanctions' or 'truce fails'.

proposals.name: Unresolved curiosity gap or implied question
proposals.rationale: Omitting key information creates a knowledge gap that heavily incentivizes the reader to click to resolve.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline teases a mystery, a hidden secret, or a rhetorical question without revealing the core fact. Scores low for explicit, complete factual summaries.

proposals.name: Geopolitical complexity or foreign diplomatic process
proposals.rationale: General readers often bypass complex geopolitical processes in favor of simpler, more relatable narratives.
proposals.description: Scores high for dense foreign diplomacy, distant institutional elections, and complex regional history. Scores low for domestic or personality-driven news.

proposals.name: Pop-culture nostalgia or retro media reference
proposals.rationale: Readers click nostalgia-triggering headlines to relive shared cultural touchstones from their youth.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline references retro pop culture, classic media, or past decades. Scores low for current affairs or breaking news.

proposals.name: Ominous but vague future threat
proposals.rationale: Vague future threats create anxiety and curiosity, compelling readers to click to assess their personal risk.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline warns of an impending but undefined crisis or 'national security threat'. Scores low for resolved events or specific facts.

proposals.name: Resolved past event or historical flashback
proposals.rationale: Readers seeking immediate news click less on historical analyses or retrospective contexts than on active stories.
proposals.description: Scores high for articles explaining past conflicts, historical territorial anomalies, or retrospective obituaries. Scores low for breaking or ongoing current events.

proposals.name: Consumer tech or everyday product hack
proposals.rationale: Everyday product vulnerabilities are highly clickable because they immediately impact the reader's personal security or property.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text highlights a flaw or hack in a recognizable consumer product. Scores low for macroeconomics or industrial policy.

proposals.name: High-emotion adversity or emotional family plea
proposals.rationale: Emotional human-interest stories about familial suffering or pleas drive strong empathetic clicking behavior.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline focuses on family grief, pleading, or profound personal tragedy. Scores low for abstract policy impacts.

proposals.name: Directly contradictory or unexpected juxtaposition
proposals.rationale: Readers click unexpected juxtapositions seeking to understand how the apparent contradiction logically resolves.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline features an ironic clash of concepts, like Catholic Malta and gay marriage. Scores low for expected, routine pairings.

proposals.name: Unintuitive causal mechanism or systemic failure
proposals.rationale: Bizarre real-world consequences of policies intrigue readers by violating normal expectations of institutional logic.
proposals.description: Scores high if a systemic action causes an unintended, dramatic real-world side effect. Scores low for predictable political outcomes.

proposals.name: Named US elite actor present
proposals.description: Headline explicitly names a current or former US politician, government institution, or major US law enforcement agency.

proposals.name: Active Anglophone celebrity quoted
proposals.description: Headline centers on a well-known English-speaking entertainment or pop-culture figure, often using quotation marks for their speech.

proposals.name: Named foreign geopolitical conflict zone
proposals.description: Headline references ongoing unrest in a non-Anglophone country, often combining a geographic proper noun with institutional or military terms.

proposals.name: UK domestic life disrupted by policy
proposals.description: Headline text describes a logistical, legal, or economic restriction affecting daily civilian life in the UK.

proposals.name: Quirky or oddity human-interest phrasing
proposals.description: Headline uses colloquialisms, puns, or eccentric framing for a non-hard-news event.

proposals.name: Running story day-count tag
proposals.description: Headline text contains ordinal day numbers or explicit references to being part of an ongoing multi-day story.

proposals.name: Headline takes analytical question form
proposals.description: Headline is formatted entirely or primarily as a question meant to explain a complex issue.

proposals.name: Headline takes feature analysis form
proposals.description: Headline begins with "Why", "How", or "What" to signal a long-form background analysis rather than breaking news.

proposals.name: Named region plus institutional action
proposals.description: Headline pairs a specific geographic location (often a developing nation) with formal verbs like urges, blocks, or delays.

proposals.name: Explicit mentions of violent victimization
proposals.description: Headline contains specific violent or sexual crime keywords like rape, killed, or trafficked.

proposals.name: Quoted Colloquialism
proposals.rationale: Casual phrasing drives curiosity and signals lighthearted, highly clickable content.
proposals.description: Headlines using informal, idiomatic, or slang phrasing in quotes score high (e.g., "wrong 'un"). Formal headlines score low. Does not apply to straight news quotes.

proposals.name: Implicit Mystery Gap
proposals.rationale: Withholding the main subject creates a curiosity gap that directly forces reader clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines deliberately omitting key information (e.g., "smack a space rock") score high. Headlines stating all facts clearly score low.

proposals.name: Prominent Western Elite Actor
proposals.rationale: BBC's domestic audience disproportionately clicks on highly familiar Western cultural figures.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring globally recognized Western politicians/celebrities score high. Unknown or non-Western figures score low. Does not apply to generic institutions.

proposals.name: Localized Geographic Exoticism
proposals.rationale: Explainer formats about unfamiliar places leverage high curiosity and broad general appeal.
proposals.description: Headlines framed as questions about unusual specific locations (e.g., "two parts of Africa") score high. Standard geopolitical news scores low.

proposals.name: Fronted Question Interrogative
proposals.rationale: Question headlines explicitly promise to resolve an information gap, strongly motivating reader clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines starting with "What", "How", or "Why" score high if they promise a direct explanation. Statements score low. Does not apply to rhetorical quotes.

proposals.name: UK/Domestic Cultural Anchor
proposals.rationale: The BBC's primary demographic clicks heavily on domestic cultural touchstones and local outrage.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring exclusively UK-centric personalities/events (e.g., Grenfell, Stormzy) score high. Foreign events score low. Does not apply to generic foreign policy.

proposals.name: Playful Alliteration or Pun
proposals.rationale: Linguistic playfulness signals a softer, entertaining read, which drives high impulse clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines with obvious wordplay (e.g., "hot tub hack") score high. Straightforward factual headlines score low. Does not apply to serious tragedies.

proposals.name: Hyperbolic Evaluative Adjective
proposals.rationale: Hyperbole amplifies emotional arousal and perceived stakes, prompting immediate reader investigation.
proposals.description: Headlines using strong subjective adjectives like "amazing", "colossal", or "unacceptable" score high. Neutral adjectives score low.

proposals.name: Lack of Public Policy Jargon
proposals.rationale: Casual readers bypass complex policy headlines, preferring accessible, human-centric daily stories.
proposals.description: Headlines avoiding complex political/institutional terms (e.g., "borrowing", "pact") score high. Jargon-heavy headlines score low.

proposals.name: Imminent Ongoing Temporality
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize clicking on dynamic, real-time events to stay updated on breaking news.
proposals.description: Headlines referencing an event actively unfolding or launching (e.g., "set for launch") score high. Past or historical events score low.

proposals.name: Bizarre Novelty Contrast
proposals.rationale: Juxtaposing normal institutional actions with absurd props creates massive cognitive dissonance and clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines combining two unexpected elements (e.g., "oath on a comic") score high. Expected pairings score low.

proposals.name: Named Western Outlets/Brands
proposals.rationale: High familiarity with consumer brands creates immediate personal relevance and triggers reader trust.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring recognizable corporate brands (Netflix, Wikipedia, Robinhood) score high. Obscure organizations score low. Does not apply to governments.

proposals.name: Outrage-Inducing Specifier
proposals.rationale: Visceral emotional triggers bypass editorial constraints to elicit strong, immediate reader clicking behavior.
proposals.description: Headlines containing vulnerable victims or shocking crimes (e.g., "stolen ashes") score high. Routine crimes score low.

proposals.name: Direct Pronoun Posessive Hook
proposals.rationale: First-person narrative intimacy signals a deeply personal, gossip-level story that drives impulse clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines leading with a first-person quote ("I can tell", "my family") score high. Third-person institutional actions score low.

proposals.name: Explicit Visceral Violence Term
proposals.rationale: Readers are psychologically wired to click on explicit physical threats and violent anomalies.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring direct physical violence words score high. Institutional terms like "fraud" or "infiltration" score low.

proposals.name: Playful or quirky phrasing
proposals.parent: Editorial curation and audience engagement strategy
proposals.description: Headline uses puns, alliteration, informal verbs, or idiomatic phrases, indicating an editorial push to make a story highly clickable.

proposals.name: Top-tier US political actor
proposals.description: Headline explicitly names major US politicians or parties, catching the articulated criteria's elite actor value regardless of UK reader demand.

proposals.name: Strong emotion or outrage markers
proposals.description: Headline features highly emotive language (e.g., "troubled", "unacceptable", "snag") or dramatic human tragedy, creating an outsize clickability signal.

proposals.name: Niche historical or cultural framing
proposals.description: Headline focuses on historical facts, explanations of borders, or abstract cultural shifts, reflecting explanatory feature writing that gets promoted but isn't urgently clicked.

proposals.name: Broad regional institutional action
proposals.description: Headline mentions general geographic regions (e.g., "Africa", "Pacific") or distant institutional conflicts lacking specific elite names, acting as broad foreign news markers.

proposals.name: Discrete geographic country name
proposals.parent: Wire copy and foreign desk templates
proposals.description: Headline features the exact name of a single foreign country, triggering domestic relevance and institutional markers without ensuring UK audience interest.

proposals.name: Direct quote from an actor
proposals.parent: PR cycle and daily interview exclusives
proposals.description: Headline consists primarily of a dramatic or bold quotation, signaling a soft news interview exclusive that editors feature prominently.

proposals.name: Soft news humanization cliché
proposals.parent: Soft news and celebrity desk quotas
proposals.description: Headline uses tropes like "America's girl next door" or "cycle of pain" signaling a glossy feature profile rather than urgent hard news.

proposals.name: Continuing running story label
proposals.description: Headline uses explicit day counters or references a ongoing multi-day narrative, marking it as a continuation rather than a novel, standalone event.

proposals.name: Royalty or UK TV celebrity name
proposals.description: Headline explicitly names UK royalty or personalities from popular British television, highly clickable to local audiences but undervalued by elite political criteria.

proposals.name: PERSONAL REVELATION
proposals.rationale: Readers click intimate psychological confessions by famous people, driving massive same-outlet engagement.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if headline explicitly describes a celebrity or elite personally revealing a secret, trauma, or taboo. Scores low for routine institutional statements. Does not apply to general news.

proposals.name: DIRECT ADDRESS OR FIRST-PERSON QUOTE
proposals.rationale: Quotes create immediate psychological proximity and urgency, increasing reader interest and subsequent clicks.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if text uses first-person perspective or quotes someone speaking directly. Scores low for indirect reported speech. Does not apply to unquoted text.

proposals.name: VIOLENT OR SEXUAL CRIME ACCUSATION
proposals.rationale: True crime and sexual scandal carry a strong morbid curiosity factor that reliably drives clicks.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high for explicit mentions of violent/sexual charges or acquittals involving named individuals. Scores low for general geopolitical conflict. Does not apply to non-crime news.

proposals.name: BUZZWORDS AND INTERNET SLANG
proposals.rationale: Informal, quirky, or tech-adjacent vocabulary signals accessible soft news, boosting reader clicks.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if headline uses highly informal, viral, or tech-internet slang (e.g., "smack", "hack", "snag"). Scores low for formal diplomatic language. Does not apply to standard journalistic phrasing.

proposals.name: HUMAN VULNERABILITY OF NON-ELITES
proposals.rationale: Bizarre emotional tragedies involving ordinary people trigger empathetic curiosity and high read-rates.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if ordinary people are victims of bizarre, emotional, or freak events. Scores low for mass statistics or institutional policies. Does not apply to elites.

proposals.name: MAJOR ONGOING CONFLICT MILESTONE
proposals.rationale: Highly salient running stories generate daily suspense; readers click chronological updates to track developments.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high for chronological updates on major, highly salient wars (e.g., Russia-Ukraine). Scores low for isolated conflicts with low domestic relevance. Does not apply to historical conflicts.

proposals.name: TABLOID FRAME OR PLAYFUL PUN
proposals.rationale: Entertaining, softly worded headlines act as click-magnets by promising a diverting, easily digestible narrative.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high for colloquial puns, jokes, or pop-culture references. Scores low for formal headlines. Does not apply to straight hard news reporting.

proposals.name: FIGUREHEAD NAME PLUS NEUTRAL ACTION
proposals.rationale: Mere presence of an elite actor is insufficient for clicks; routine institutional actions bore readers.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low if headline features a famous person doing something routine or institutional. Scores high if doing something deeply personal. Does not apply to non-celebrities.

proposals.name: OBSCURE FOREIGN POLICY MECHANICS
proposals.rationale: Readers routinely ignore distant institutional diplomacy in favor of immediate domestic or highly violent crises.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low if detailing complex, distant geopolitical treaties or borders. Scores high if featuring recognizable, immediate crises. Does not apply to domestic politics.

proposals.name: NON-VIOLENT DOMESTIC POLITICAL STATEMENT
proposals.rationale: Routine political posturing lacks the novelty or stakes necessary to motivate a reader to click.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for domestic politicians merely giving warnings or making administrative rulings. Scores high for elections or scandals. Does not apply to international relations.

proposals.name: DOMESTIC ECONOMIC FORECAST OR STATISTIC
proposals.rationale: Readers click economics that immediately affect their wallets, bypassing abstract macroeconomic financial updates.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for abstract financial updates, borrowing figures, or market warnings. Scores high for personal finance impacts. Does not apply to corporate business news.

proposals.name: EXTREME WEATHER OR ENVIRONMENTAL STATISTIC
proposals.rationale: Distant ecological statistics lack the immediate threat level required to trigger high same-outlet readership.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for slow-moving environmental data or distant climate reports. Scores high for immediate, local disasters. Does not apply to conservation successes.

proposals.name: FORMAL LEGAL PROCEDURE DELAY
proposals.rationale: Readers seek closure and drama in legal stories, largely ignoring intermediate procedural updates.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for routine court procedural delays, continuances, or scheduling. Scores high for final verdicts or dramatic trials. Does not apply to criminal investigations.

proposals.name: UNFAMILIAR FOREIGN PROPER NOUN DOMINANCE
proposals.rationale: Headline alienation occurs when readers lack mental schemas for obscure geopolitical actors, suppressing clicks.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low if subjects are unfamiliar foreign institutions or non-elite regional figures. Scores high if featuring globally recognized entities. Does not apply to domestic names.

proposals.name: LOW-STAKES CULTURAL HUMAN INTEREST
proposals.rationale: Clicks favor broad, easily understood cultural narratives over specialized features requiring high prior knowledge.
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for niche arts, obscure history, or minor community projects. Scores high for major celebrity entertainment. Does not apply to hard news.

proposals.name: Serial story day counter
proposals.description: Headline explicitly denotes an ongoing multi-day event via a numbered day or ordinal term.

proposals.name: Literal direct quote marks
proposals.parent: Editorial preference for soft-news or interview formatting
proposals.description: Headline contains verbatim quotation marks indicating direct speech, opinion, or a subjective descriptor.

proposals.name: Casual or sensational colloquialism
proposals.description: Uses informal, slang, or highly evocative vocabulary (e.g., "smack," "snag," "wolf") uncommon in standard hard news.

proposals.name: Analytical interrogative format
proposals.parent: Editorial push for evergreen context or analysis pieces
proposals.description: Opens with a question word (e.g., "How," "Why") implying an explanatory or analytical article.

proposals.name: Geographic curiosity framing
proposals.description: Uses phrases like "The country that..." or highlights an obscure geographic territory as a curiosity.

proposals.name: Event ordinality or resolution verb
proposals.parent: Position within a multi-day news cycle
proposals.description: Contains explicit language marking a sequence's conclusion or continuation (e.g., "finally," "now," "delays," "remains").

proposals.name: Celebrity hook on hard news
proposals.parent: SEO or cross-platform traffic optimization strategy
proposals.description: Headlines lead strictly with a recognizable entertainment or sports figure to anchor a broader social issue.

proposals.name: Hyper-specific human-interest detail
proposals.description: Lead framing relies on idiosyncratic, granular descriptors (e.g., "Canadian grandma," "drive-through") rather than broad stakes.

proposals.name: Puzzling standalone elliptical headline
proposals.parent: Homepage placement alongside large visual assets
proposals.description: Highly compressed, ambiguous phrasing lacking context (e.g., "Collapse 'felt like an earthquake'").

proposals.name: Explicit fact-checking label
proposals.parent: Mandated editorial format for disinformation beats
proposals.description: Contains in-house terminology such as "Fact-checked," "Explained," or "Analysis" to denote article format.
